To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the levels of Cu and Fe in blood, liver and spleen of zinc deficient rats were significantly lower as compared with those in pair-fed rats.

the element levels (including zinc, copper, iron, manganese, and calcium) in blood, organs, and fetuses of rats were significantly lower in zinc-deficient rats than in zinc-supplemented and control rats.
the distribution of minerals induced by zinc deficiency in maternal tissues might be different from that in fetuses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of zinc deficiency on mineral metabolism of pregnant rats and fetuses.

the influence of zinc deficiency on distribution of elements in tissue of pregnant rats, and the results may provide some references for the study on the mechanism of mineral metabolism and the prevention of zinc deficiency.
the influence of zinc deficiency on mineral distribution in the tissues of rats and their fetusses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the deficiency of Zn would cause a decrease in the level of elements in maternal tissues and fetuses.
the distribution of elements is affected by zinc deficiency.

the distribution of elements induced by zinc deficiency in pregnant rats and their fetus was different, and the decrease was not only due to the reduction of dietary intakes caused by zinc deficiency, but also to the competition and coordination of elements in the intestinal absorption, placental transport, and the metabolism of organs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distribution of Zn in tissues is closely related to other minerals.
the distribution of elements induced by zinc deficiency is different from those of pair-fed rats, and the distribution of minerals between maternal tissue and fetuses may be different.
zinc deficiency may influence the distribution of minerals and elements in maternal and fetal tissues, and the influence is different in different tissues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
zinc deficiency in pregnant rats can cause the reduction of mineral content in maternal blood, organs and fetal organs, and the change of distribution of elements in maternal and fetal tissues.

the decrease of elements content in maternal tissues induced zinc deficiency may be not mainly due to the reduction of dietary element intake, but the competition between elements in intestinal absorption and the coordination relationships in tissue distribution.
